result.markdown: --- title: "[Graph.rich_club_coefficient()]{.doc-object-name .doc-function .doc-label .doc-label-method}" body-classes: doc-api-page doc-py-api-page shift-heading-level-by: 0 toc-depth: 3 page-navigation: false html-table-processing: none --- ::: {.doc-subject} Compute the rich-club coefficient for all degree values. ::: ::: {.doc-usage-source} Usage [Source](https://github.com/rich-iannone/edgecase/blob/main/python/edgecase/graph.py#L32675-L32761){target="_blank" rel="noopener"} ::: ::: {.doc-signature .doc-Kind.FUNCTION} ```python Graph.rich_club_coefficient() ``` ::: ::: {.doc-text} ![Rich-club coefficient](/assets/graphs/rich-club-coefficient.light.svg){.lightbox fig-alt="A five-node graph whose three degree-3 nodes B, C, D are grouped in the accent color and fully linked to each other. The table gives, for each degree k, the nodes above k, the edges among them, and phi(k): 0.6, 0.833, and 1.0 at k = 2." width="100%"} The rich-club coefficient `φ(k)` measures the connectivity among high-degree nodes (the 'rich club' of the network). For each degree `k`, it computes the ratio of actual edges to potential edges among nodes with degree greater than `k`: `\\phi(k) = \\frac{2E_k}{N_k(N_k - 1)}` where: - `N_k` is the number of nodes with degree > k - `E_k` is the number of edges among those nodes A rich-club coefficient close to `1` indicates that high-degree nodes tend to be connected to each other, forming a 'rich club'. Values less than expected in random graphs suggest the hubs avoid connecting to each other. ::: ## Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [dict[int, float]]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : Dictionary mapping degree `k` to rich-club coefficient `φ(k)`. Only degrees for which at least `2` nodes have degree > `k` are included (otherwise the coefficient is undefined). ::: ## Technical Notes {.doc-technical-notes} For each degree threshold $k$, the coefficient is $\phi(k) = \dfrac{2\, E_{>k}}{N_{>k}(N_{>k} - 1)}$, the observed density among nodes with degree strictly above $k$. Self-loops and edge weights are excluded; for directed graphs the threshold applies to total degree. A rising $\phi(k)$ curve suggests that hubs preferentially wire to other hubs, the classic rich-club effect first characterized by Zhou and Mondragón (2004). The raw values returned here are *unnormalized*, which matters because $\phi(k)$ trivially approaches $1$ near the top of the degree spectrum: so few nodes remain to divide by. To decide whether a real rich-club signal is present, compare against $\phi_{\mathrm{rand}}(k)$ computed on a degree-preserving randomization of the graph and inspect the ratio $\phi(k)/\phi_{\mathrm{rand}}(k)$. ## Examples {.doc-examples} Analyze hub connectivity in a network: ::: {#55967935 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import edgecase as ec # Create a network with clear hub structure graph = ( ec.Graph() .add_nodes(["hub1", "hub2", "hub3", "spoke1", "spoke2", "spoke3"]) .add_edges( [ # Connect hubs to each other (rich club) ("hub1", "hub2"), ("hub2", "hub3"), ("hub3", "hub1"), # Connect spokes to hubs ("hub1", "spoke1"), ("hub2", "spoke2"), ("hub3", "spoke3"), ] ) ) rc = graph.rich_club_coefficient() # Returns rich club coefficients dict # Higher values at larger k indicate hubs prefer connecting to each other rc ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` {0: 0.4, 2: 1.0, 1: 1.0} ``` ::: ::: Compare with random network: ::: {#6365c28a .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} # Scale-free networks often show rich-club phenomenon ba_graph = ec.Graph().add_pa_graph(100, 3) rc = ba_graph.rich_club_coefficient() # Check if high-degree nodes are more interconnected than expected # Filter coefficients > 0.5 to see strong rich-club effect {k: phi for k, phi in rc.items() if phi > 0.5} ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=2} ``` {11: 0.5333333333333333, 14: 0.7333333333333333, 22: 1.0, 17: 1.0, 25: 1.0, 20: 1.0, 12: 0.5714285714285714, 23: 1.0, 15: 0.8, 18: 1.0, 21: 1.0, 13: 0.7333333333333333, 24: 1.0, 16: 1.0, 19: 1.0} ``` ::: :::
